learning_goal: Draw the three boundaries and the floor of the femoral triangle, list its contents in the NAVEL order from lateral to medial, say where the femoral artery begins and ends, and explain why a femoral hernia sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle while an inguinal hernia sits above and medial to it.

terms: nerve artery vein empty space lymphatics

structures.name: right inguinal ligament
structures.label: Inguinal ligament — the base
structures.narration: The rolled-under lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It is the base of the triangle and the line everything in the groin is described against. Learn its two ends: the femoral artery enters at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, and a femoral hernia appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

structures.name: right sartorius
structures.label: Sartorius — lateral border
structures.narration: It leaves the anterior superior iliac spine and runs down and inwards across the thigh. Its medial border is the lateral wall of the triangle. Note the trick in the wording: the lateral boundary is the medial border of sartorius, and the medial boundary is the medial border of adductor longus. Examiners ask for the border, not just the muscle.

structures.name: right adductor longus
structures.label: Adductor longus — medial border
structures.narration: From the front of the body of the pubis to the middle of the linea aspera. Its medial border is the medial wall of the triangle, and its upper surface helps make the floor as well — the same muscle does both jobs. Where sartorius crosses over it, the two borders meet and the triangle ends: that meeting point is the apex.

structures.name: right psoas major
structures.label: Psoas major — floor, lateral part
structures.narration: Psoas comes down out of the abdomen behind the inguinal ligament and joins iliacus as iliopsoas. Together they form the lateral half of the floor. Because the muscle runs from the lumbar spine straight into the thigh, pus from a tuberculous lumbar spine can track down its sheath and point in the femoral triangle as a cold abscess.

structures.name: right iliacus
structures.label: Iliacus — floor, lateral part
structures.narration: The fan filling the iliac fossa, joining psoas to reach the lesser trochanter. The femoral nerve lies in the groove between the two muscles, on the floor and behind the fascia — which is why the nerve is outside the femoral sheath while the artery and vein are inside it.

structures.name: right pectineus
structures.label: Pectineus — floor, medial part
structures.narration: A flat quadrilateral from the pecten pubis to the femur just below the lesser trochanter. It makes the middle of the floor, between iliopsoas laterally and adductor longus medially. Recite the floor from lateral to medial as iliopsoas, pectineus, adductor longus and you have it in the order you see it.

structures.name: right external iliac artery
structures.label: Femoral artery (continuous with the external iliac artery)
structures.narration: One vessel, two names. The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery the moment it passes behind the inguinal ligament, and there is no join to find — the catalog holds the abdominal length of it, so read the lower end as the femoral artery in the triangle. It is the most lateral of the three structures in the sheath, it gives off the profunda femoris about four centimetres below the ligament, and it is the vessel you feel at the mid-inguinal point and puncture for arterial access.

structures.name: right external iliac vein
structures.label: Femoral vein (continuous with the external iliac vein)
structures.narration: The same rule on the venous side: the femoral vein becomes the external iliac vein at the inguinal ligament. It lies medial to the artery at the base of the triangle but slips behind it lower down, so the level at which you look changes the answer. The great saphenous vein joins its front through the saphenous opening about four centimetres below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

structures.name: right femur
structures.label: Femur
structures.narration: The head and neck of the femur lie directly behind the triangle, separated from the vessels only by iliopsoas and the hip joint capsule. That is why a hip joint effusion is felt as fullness in the groin and why the femoral vessels are at risk in anterior approaches to the hip.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: Two landmarks on this bone define everything in the groin: the anterior superior iliac spine laterally and the pubic tubercle medially. Every hernia, every pulse and every needle in this region is described by its position relative to those two points.

structures.name: right vastus medialis
structures.label: Vastus medialis
structures.narration: It appears at the apex of the triangle and becomes the anterolateral wall of the adductor canal below it. The triangle does not end the vessels — it hands them on.

structures.name: right adductor brevis
structures.label: Adductor brevis
structures.narration: It lies behind pectineus and adductor longus, out of the triangle but immediately deep to its medial floor. The two divisions of the obturator nerve sandwich it, which is the landmark for the nerve in the medial compartment.

structures.label: Anterior superior iliac spine
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT, the lateral end of the inguinal ligament (gap 0.09 mm on a 208 mm bone); tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --contact FMA21964. Checked against a second, independent witness — the origin of sartorius (gap 0.49 mm) — which lands 9.9 mm away, 4.8% of the bone's span, so the two structures the spine is defined by agree. This is the same coordinate gross__pelvis-perineum__bony-pelvis already carries for the right ASIS, re-derived here rather than copied.
structures.narration: The lateral end of the inguinal ligament and the origin of sartorius, in the same place because they are the same corner of bone. It is the point you measure limb length from and one of the two ends of every line drawn across the groin.

structures.label: Pubic tubercle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT, the medial end of the inguinal ligament (gap 0.52 mm), restricted to the lower third of the bone so the search cannot return the lateral end; tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --contact FMA21964 --slab z:0,0.35. Two independent checks: it lies 134 mm from the measured ASIS, a credible length for the inguinal ligament on a 208 mm hip bone, and 14 mm from the origin of adductor longus on the body of the pubis, which is where that origin belongs relative to the tubercle.
structures.narration: The single most useful bony point in the groin. A femoral hernia comes out below and lateral to it; an inguinal hernia lies above and medial. The saphenofemoral junction is about four centimetres below and lateral to it. Every one of those statements is a direction from this point, so find it first.

structures.label: Pecten pubis (pectineal line)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT with --area 3, the middle of the patch where pectineus takes origin (nearest gap 0.04 mm, 38 vertices in the patch, centroid snapped 2.49 mm to the surface); tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --contact FMA22450 --area 3. --area is used because the pecten is a line of origin, not a point, so the nearest single vertex would land at one end of it. It sits 13 mm lateral to the measured pubic tubercle, which is the direction the pecten runs.
terms: posterior wall of the femoral ring
structures.narration: The sharp ridge running back and laterally from the pubic tubercle. Pectineus arises along it, and it is the hard posterior wall of the femoral ring — one of the two rigid edges that make a femoral hernia strangulate.

views.title: Find the triangle
views.narration: The femoral triangle is a hollow in the upper third of the front of the thigh, just below the groin crease. It is not a structure — it is a space, and its whole value is that it tells you what lies where when you put a hand or a needle into the groin. Point down, base up.

views.title: The three boundaries
views.narration: Above, the inguinal ligament forms the base. Laterally, the medial border of sartorius. Medially, the medial border of adductor longus. Three lines, one space. Say them in that order — base, lateral, medial — and you will never leave one out. The two lit points are the ends of the base: the anterior superior iliac spine laterally and the pubic tubercle medially, both measured on the bone rather than estimated.

views.title: Where the apex is
views.narration: Follow sartorius downwards and it crosses over adductor longus. Where the two borders meet is the apex, roughly a hand's breadth below the inguinal ligament. Below the apex the space does not close — it becomes the adductor canal, and the same vessels simply carry on.

views.title: The floor, from lateral to medial
views.narration: The floor is a gutter, not a flat sheet. Iliopsoas fills the lateral half, pectineus the middle, adductor longus the medial edge. The dip between iliopsoas and pectineus is the trough the femoral vessels lie in, and it is why the pulse is felt in a definite line rather than anywhere in the groin.

views.title: NAVEL — the order of the contents
views.narration: From lateral to medial under the inguinal ligament: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics. NAVEL. The femoral nerve is the outermost and the only one outside the femoral sheath. Then the artery, then the vein, then the femoral canal with its fat and a lymph node, and the deep inguinal nodes most medially. Get the order right and the femoral pulse tells you where every other structure is.

views.title: Trace the artery through
views.narration: The external iliac artery comes down inside the pelvis, passes behind the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point — halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, not the midpoint of the ligament itself, which lies further laterally and marks the deep inguinal ring — and is called the femoral artery from that moment. It crosses the floor of the triangle, gives the profunda femoris from its back and lateral side about four centimetres down, and leaves at the apex into the adductor canal. Two landmarks worth memorising: the mid-inguinal point for the pulse, and the profunda origin, because that is the branch that supplies most of the thigh.

views.title: Artery and vein, and which is where
views.narration: At the base of the triangle the vein is medial to the artery. At the apex it has moved behind it. That single fact is the reason a femoral venous line is aimed a finger's breadth medial to the pulse and aimed high, close to the ligament, where the vein is still beside the artery rather than under it.

views.title: The nerve on the floor
views.narration: The path traced here is the femoral nerve, L2, L3 and L4. It forms inside psoas major, runs down in the groove between psoas and iliacus, and enters the thigh lateral to the artery and behind the iliac fascia rather than in the femoral sheath. About four centimetres below the ligament it explodes into its anterior and posterior divisions. That short trunk is why a femoral nerve block is placed high, just below the ligament and just lateral to the pulse.

views.title: A cut just below the ligament
views.narration: Slide the cut down from the ligament to the apex. High up the space is wide and the vessels sit side by side on iliopsoas and pectineus. As the cut descends, sartorius swings across the front, the vein tucks behind the artery, and the wide triangle narrows into the tunnel of the adductor canal. The femoral sheath itself is a funnel of transversalis and iliac fascia dragged down from the abdomen, and it ends about three centimetres in.

views.title: The femoral canal and the hernia
views.narration: Medial to the vein, inside the sheath, is the femoral canal — a short space of fat and one lymph node that exists so the vein can expand. Its mouth, the femoral ring, is bounded in front by the inguinal ligament, behind by the pecten pubis, medially by the lacunar ligament and laterally by the vein. It is narrow and its edges are sharp, so a femoral hernia through it strangulates early. Distinguish it at the bedside by the pubic tubercle: femoral hernias lie below and lateral to it, inguinal hernias above and medial.

views.title: Why the groin nodes matter
views.narration: The path traced here is lymph leaving the groin. Superficial inguinal nodes lie in the fat below the ligament and take the whole lower limb, the perineum, the lower anal canal, the vulva or scrotal skin and the abdominal wall below the umbilicus. They drain into the deep inguinal nodes along the vein, the highest of which sits in the femoral canal and is called Cloquet's node. So enlarged groin nodes are a reason to examine the leg, the anus and the genitalia, not just the leg.

views.title: Peel down to the space
views.narration: The dissection order to recite: skin, then superficial fascia holding the superficial inguinal nodes and the great saphenous vein, then the fascia lata with its saphenous opening, then the femoral sheath with the artery and vein inside it, then the floor muscles with the femoral nerve lying on them. Learn the roof and the floor as layers and the contents have an address rather than a list.

gaps: There is no femoral artery or femoral vein in the catalog. Both are taught through the vessel they are continuous with — the external iliac artery and vein — because the femoral vessels are the same tubes under a different name below the inguinal ligament, and no join exists to mislead a student. The labels say so explicitly. The consequence is that the modelled length lies mostly above the ligament, so the intra-triangle course is narrated and traced rather than shown at full length.

The profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh) and its origin about four centimetres below the inguinal ligament are not modelled. This is the branch that supplies most of the thigh and the one that makes the difference between a common and a superficial femoral artery in a report, so it is named in narration on the artery and in the trace beat.

No nerve of the lower limb exists as a model. The femoral nerve — the N of NAVEL and the most lateral content — is authored as a traced concept path from psoas major through the groove with iliacus and under the inguinal ligament to the muscles it supplies. Its root value, its position outside the femoral sheath and its early branching are narration only.

No lymph node or lymphatic vessel is modelled anywhere in the catalog, so the superficial and deep inguinal groups and Cloquet's node in the femoral canal are taught as a traced concept path plus narration. This scene therefore does not claim to cover any lymph node curriculum entry.

The femoral sheath, the femoral canal and the femoral ring are fascial spaces with no mesh. They are the clinical heart of the region, so they are taught by lighting the vein and the pecten pubis of the hip bone and describing the four walls of the ring. A modelled sheath would be the single most valuable addition to this scene.

The great saphenous vein and the saphenous opening in the fascia lata are not in the catalog, so the saphenofemoral junction is described by its landmark — four centimetres below and lateral to the pubic tubercle — rather than shown.

The fascia lata itself has no mesh on this side of the thigh, so the roof of the triangle is narrated. The iliotibial tract exists but is a lateral structure and would misrepresent the roof if used for it.

The pubic tubercle, the pecten pubis and the anterior superior iliac spine were listed here as unmeasured sub-features of the whole hip bone mesh. That note was stale: FMA16586 is in the local decimated set, and all three were measured at this audit and are now anchors — the ASIS on two converging witnesses (sartorius and the lateral end of the inguinal ligament, 9.9 mm apart), the pubic tubercle as the medial end of the inguinal ligament within the lower third of the bone, and the pecten pubis as the pectineus contact patch. All three are status needs-review until someone opens the scene and looks at where they landed. The femoral ring's other two walls, the lacunar ligament and the vein, are still not marked: the ligament has no mesh and a wall is not a point.

The femoral sheath's lateral, intermediate and medial compartments have no meshes, so beat 10 lights the measured pecten pubis and the pubic tubercle as the two bony walls of the femoral ring and names the other two. The ring itself is not drawn.
